doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Low pay for jazz gigs and the Baked Potato
summary: Jazz brunches still pay $30-40 as in the 70s, and clubs pay a cut of the door.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: If you had a 3-hour jazz brunch gig in Los Angeles, what’s the average musician get paid for something like that these days?

Well let me think back to the 70s. Same thing. You get hardly anything. Yeah, it might pay $30 a musician, or $40. Now back in the 70s that was about a quarter or a third of your rent. Now if your rent’s $1000 instead of $150, now that gig should pay a third of your rent, which is $300 or something, but it still pays 30, 40 dollars. Most jazz gigs, it doesn’t matter if it’s a brunch or a jazz club. Some jazz clubs you still get the door.
Yeah. I think I was out there probably 15 years ago, at the Baked Potato or something.
The Baked Potato. I live a couple of miles down. You still get the door.
They what? They get the door?

They get the door. And it’s not even the whole door, it’s 80% of the door. So it’s not enough that they don’t pay you, they still want a cut of the door. And so I used to play there, but no, I can’t call musicians anymore, the kind that I want, and say it’s the door or it’s $30 or it’s $40. I just can’t make that call.
